### Weather and Environmental Instruments {#sec-weather-iv}

Weather is the most obviously exogenous variable an applied researcher will ever meet. Nobody
chooses the rainfall, the wind direction, or the temperature, so the independence assumption that
costs so much argument elsewhere comes free. That is exactly why the family is dangerous: the
assumption that weather is randomly assigned is true and irrelevant, because the assumption that
does the work is the exclusion restriction, and weather fails it more often than any other
instrument in common use.

#### The Canonical Designs

@miguel2004economic instrument economic growth with rainfall to estimate the effect of income on
civil conflict in sub-Saharan Africa, on the logic that rainfall drives agricultural output in
rain-fed economies and affects conflict only through income. @madestam2013political instrument
protest turnout with rainfall on the day of a scheduled rally. @deryugina2019mortality instrument
local air pollution with daily changes in wind direction, which is the most defensible member of
the family because wind direction plausibly affects health only by moving pollutants.
@dell2014what survey the broader climate-economy literature.

The construction is always the same: weather shifts a mediating variable, and the analyst asserts
that it touches the outcome through no other route.

#### The Problem, Made Concrete

```{r wxiv-demo, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ivreg)
set.seed(606)

wx <- function(n = 2000, direct = 0) {
  rain <- rnorm(n)
  conf <- rnorm(n)                                  # unobserved confounder
  income   <- -0.8 * rain + conf + rnorm(n)         # rain moves income
  # True effect of income on conflict is -0.5. `direct` is an excluded channel:
  # rainfall reaching conflict without going through income.
  conflict <- -0.5 * income + direct * rain + 0.7 * conf + rnorm(n)
  d <- data.frame(conflict, income, rain)
  c(IV_estimate  = unname(coef(ivreg(conflict ~ income | rain, data = d))[2]),
    first_stage_F = unname(summary(lm(income ~ rain, data = d))$fstatistic[1]))
}

tab <- t(sapply(c(0, 0.1, 0.3), function(dd)
  c(direct_channel = dd, round(rowMeans(replicate(300, wx(direct = dd))), 2))))
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste("Rainfall as an instrument for income. The true effect of",
                  "income on conflict is -0.50. direct_channel is the size of a",
                  "pathway from rainfall to conflict that bypasses income."))
```

With no excluded channel the estimator is exact. A direct pathway of 0.1, one eighth the size of
the first-stage coefficient, moves the estimate from -0.50 to roughly -0.63, a twenty-five percent
overstatement. At 0.3 the estimate is nearly double the truth.

The column to stare at is the first-stage $F$. It is around 640 in every row, entirely unmoved by
the violation. This is the same lesson as Section \@ref(sec-lewbel-heteroskedasticity) in a
different setting, and it is the single most important thing to understand about weather
instruments: they are almost always strong, strength is what gets reported, and strength is
uninformative about the assumption that actually matters.

#### Why Weather Is Especially Prone to This

Rainfall does not only move agricultural income. It moves the passability of roads, which affects
the logistics of an insurgency. It affects disease vectors, school attendance, water availability,
and the ability of a government to project force. @sarsons2015rainfall makes the argument
empirically rather than rhetorically: she studies Indian districts downstream of dams, where
rainfall shocks do not pass through to local income because the dam smooths water supply. If the
exclusion restriction held, rainfall should have no effect on conflict in those districts. It
does. The first stage is shut off and the reduced form survives, which is direct evidence of an
excluded channel.

That test generalizes, and it is the strongest thing a weather-instrument paper can do. Find a
subpopulation where the proposed mechanism is blocked, and show the reduced form disappears there.
The book discusses this class of check under no-first-stage samples in
Section \@ref(sec-exclusion-evidence).

The second problem is a literature-level one rather than a paper-level one.
@mellon2025rain catalogues the treatments that weather has been used to instrument across
published work, and the list runs to hundreds: income, conflict, protest, turnout, media
consumption, mood, crime, migration, schooling, trade. Any single paper's exclusion argument is
an argument that weather affects its outcome through one channel. The union of the literature is
a demonstration that weather affects almost everything through many channels. The two positions
cannot both be right, and the aggregate evidence is against the individual claims.

#### What Distinguishes the Good Applications

@deryugina2019mortality is the family's strongest member, and the reasons are instructive. The
instrument is daily wind direction rather than a weather variable with obvious economic content,
and it is used within a location so that fixed effects absorb the average conditions of a place.
Wind direction shifts which pollution reaches a county without changing anything else about that
county on that day. The paper also documents what wind direction does and does not correlate with,
rather than asserting the exclusion restriction.

The contrast with rainfall-for-income is the degree of separation between the instrument and the
outcome. Rainfall is a first-order determinant of life in an agricultural economy. Wind direction
is close to a nuisance parameter except through the pollutants it carries.

#### Practice

1.  Do not report the first-stage $F$ as though it addressed the exclusion restriction. It does
    not, and in this family it never will.
2.  Enumerate the other channels explicitly and in writing. A referee will, and the list is
    usually long.
3.  Find a no-first-stage subsample and show the reduced form vanishes there. This is the closest
    thing to a test the design admits.
4.  Use a bounded sensitivity analysis in the style of Section \@ref(sec-plausibly-exogenous),
    and report the direct effect that would overturn the result.
5.  Prefer instruments with less economic content: wind direction over rainfall, daily variation
    over annual, within-location over cross-location.
6.  Check whether the same instrument has been used for your outcome, or a close relative of it,
    as a treatment elsewhere. If it has, the exclusion argument has to explain why that literature
    is wrong.
